title: Astronauts photographed a volcano erupting through a hole in the clouds
body: On 12 June 2009 a lucky orbit carried the International Space Station over Sarychev Peak, on Matua Island in the Kuril Islands north-east of Japan, early in its eruption. The photos show a column of brown ash and white steam topped by a smooth white **pileus** cloud, perhaps water that condensed as the air above rose fast and cooled, and a dense grey cloud hugging the slopes that was probably a pyroclastic flow, an avalanche of hot ash and gas. All around, the cloud deck has a round hole, and scientists still disagree about why.

cover.alt: Seen from orbit, a brown ash column topped by a smooth white cloud cap rises from an island through a round gap in a white cloud deck
cover.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center · Public domain

slides.alt: Looking down from orbit, a column of brown ash and steam rises from a volcanic island, capped by a smooth white dome of cloud; grey ash spreads down the slopes, and the white cloud deck around the island has a wide circular gap. The view shifts slightly from frame to frame.
slides.caption: Sarychev Peak on 12 June 2009, in a sequence of photos taken from the International Space Station as it passed overhead early in the eruption.
slides.credit: ISS Crew Earth Observations, NASA Johnson Space Center · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: How the smooth white cap on the plume may have formed

steps.label: The air above it is pushed up fast
The rising air cools and its water condenses
A smooth, short-lived pileus cloud forms

slides.prompt: Did the eruption punch that round hole in the clouds?
slides.detail: Since the photo was published, scientists have proposed three explanations, and they still disagree about which is right.

slides.heading: Three ideas for the hole
items: The island lifts the moist air, and the clouds evaporate
The eruption’s shockwave shoved the cloud deck aside
Air sinking around the ash column warmed and dried it

slides.question: What was the dense grey cloud hugging the volcano’s slopes probably made of?
slides.explanation: It was probably a pyroclastic flow: a dense cloud of hot ash and gas that pours down a volcano’s slopes instead of rising.
